sections.content: How exposed are mortgage holders and renters in Wales to rising housing costs?
The exposure scores for Wales are (very low) for mortgage holders and (very low) for renters.

What do the exposure scores mean?

In Wales, 13.8% of all households are estimated to have seen mortgage costs rise in 2023, with an average rise of £118 a month.

A further 6.5% of households are estimated to have seen their rents rise in 2023, with an average increase of £79 a month.

Housing costs presented in this article are estimates. Visit our methodology for more information on how we calculate local area exposure scores.

Mortgage holders in Wales are at very low exposure to rising housing costs

An estimated 13.8% of households in Wales experienced rising mortgage costs in 2023.

This is 170th of all 331 local authorities in England and Wales.

Overall % of households had an outstanding mortgage in this area at Census 2021.

Between autumn 2021 and summer 2023, the Bank of England's monetary policy committee raised their case rate from 0.10% to 5.25%.

This was in response to inflation rising to a 40-year high in the year to October 2022, according to the Consumer Prices Index including owner-occupier housing costs.

Mortgage-holders coming to the end of a fixed term in 2023 have been faced with higher costs as a result.

Those in Wales experiencing rising mortgage costs are estimated to have seen average increases of £118, from £543 in 2022 to £661 in 2023.

Combined, these measures give Wales a very low overall exposure score for mortgage holders of out of out of 7.

Rising costs are not spread evenly across mortgage holders in Wales.

The amount it costs to remortgage depends on several factors, including interest rates at the time, loan to value ratio, outstanding mortgage amount, and the remaining term.

For example, a household coming off a five-year fixed-rate mortgage in January 2023 would have seen a lower cost increase, at an estimated £70. This would equate to 2.8% of average household disposable income.

Those coming off a two-year fixed-rate mortgage in November 2023 would have seen higher rises in their monthly repayments, increasing by an estimated £187, or 2.8% of average household disposable income.

Mortgage-holders who may be the most protected from rising costs are those who have a lower loan amount, including those who bought when prices were lower or have had more time to pay off their mortgage.

Households headed by older people are more likely to have paid off more of their mortgage and be less exposed to rising housing costs.

According to the English Housing Survey 2022-23, 73.4% of all households headed by someone aged 65 years and over owner their property outright.

Renters in Wales are at very low exposure to rising housing costs

An estimated 6.5% of households in Wales experienced rising rents from private landlords in 2023.

This is 84th of all 331 local authorities in England and Wales.

The national picture

London is particularly impacted by rising housing costs.

Among London boroughs, the most common exposure score for rents was 7, with 90.9% of local authorities assigned this score.

The most common exposure score for mortgages was 4, at 54.5% of local authorities.
